newsitem.title: RUSSIA: SOCCER-RUSSIAN LEAGUE TELLS RIVAL CSKAS TO SETTLE ROW.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-RUSSIAN LEAGUE TELLS RIVAL CSKAS TO SETTLE ROW.

text.p: The Russian soccer league said on Wednesday it had given the Army Central Sports Club (CSKA) until March 1 to settle an internal row that has left two rival teams bidding for CSKA Moscow's spot in the 1997 premiership.

Anatoly Gorokhovsky, head of the league's disciplinary committee which met on Tuesday, told Reuters that if the army club failed to sort out its problems CSKA might find themselves out of the premier league when the new season opened on March 15.
"They have to sit down together and reach a joint decision. You can't have two sponsors," he said.
"If this goes on we could have a deadlock and reach the point where there will be no CSKA at all."

On Tuesday, the Russian Football Union (RFS), which oversees all soccer in Russia, said its disciplinary committee had ruled in favour of the CSKA Moscow squad being trained by Alexander Tarkhanov, who coached them to fifth place last season.

But the army, in the form of CSKA sports chief Colonel Alexander Baranovsky, sacked Tarkhanov at the New Year and brought in former Russian national coach Pavel Sadyrin, who was fired by Zenit St Petersburg at the end of last season.
Baranovsky says the army still controls 60 percent of the shares in the CSKA Moscow soccer club. But Tarkhanov says his backer, Moscow businessman Oleg Kim, has a 68 percent majority.
Most of last year's CSKA squad is training with Tarkhanov.
It seems likely that the matter will go to court in a virtual re-run of a a monumental falling out at CSKA's ice hockey club.
Baranovsky and the army came off worse in that clash with Viktor Tikhonov, who coached the world-beating Soviet hockey sides of the 1980s.

A series of legal battles left Tikhonov in charge of the CSKA Moscow team which takes part in the top Russian ice hockey league and in European competition. A separate CSKA team controlled by Baranovsky competes at a lower level.
